On Mercury, the Sun's closest planet, why does water ice survive four-hundred-and-thirty-degree heat? The ice hides in polar craters that never see sunlight. At fifty-eight million kilometres out, sunlight shines up to seven times brighter than on Earth, yet without an atmosphere to retain heat you would feel night plunge to minus one hundred and eighty degrees Celsius.

In 1965, Italian mathematician Giuseppe Colombo solved its spin mystery: Mercury rotates on its axis three times — once every fifty-nine Earth days — for every two eighty-eight-day orbits, so one solar day lasts one hundred and seventy-six Earth days, just over two Mercury years.

With a radius of two thousand four hundred and forty kilometres — a blueberry beside an Earth nickel — Mercury is the second densest planet because a metallic core fills about eighty-five per cent of its radius. With almost no axial tilt, deep polar craters stay in permanent shadow, where MESSENGER — orbiting Mercury from March 2011 to April 2015 — verified water ice inside Prokofiev crater. Why is Venus hotter?

At one hundred and eight million kilometres out orbits Venus, nearly Earth's twin in size. What would you see dropping beneath its sulfuric-acid clouds?

You reach the hottest planetary surface in our Solar System: a runaway greenhouse under a ninety-six point five per cent carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat and bakes the rock to four hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. Surface air crushes at ninety-two bars — like nine hundred and thirty metres underwater on Earth.

However, Venus spins backwards every two hundred and forty-three Earth days while orbiting in two hundred and twenty-five days, so the Sun rises in the west. In 1978, Pioneer Venus found deuterium at one hundred times Earth's ratio, evidence that Venus once held much more water. On 1 March 1982, Soviet lander Venera 13 survived one hundred and twenty-seven minutes — nearly four times its thirty-two-minute design. Why did Earth keep its oceans?

At one hundred and fifty million kilometres — one astronomical unit — orbits Earth, the largest rocky planet. What secret shields our oceans?

Tilted twenty-three point four degrees, Earth spins every twenty-four hours. At the equator, the surface moves at about one thousand six hundred and seventy kilometres per hour — more than four times the four-hundred-and-eight-kilometre-per-hour gust measured during Cyclone Olivia. Rotation makes Earth forty-three kilometres wider across the equator than pole to pole.

Some three thousand kilometres beneath our feet, below the rocky mantle, begins Earth's swirling liquid-iron outer core, generating a magnetic shield that flipped one hundred and eighty-three times in eighty-three million years. German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss introduced absolute magnetic-intensity measurements in the 1830s; over the past two centuries, ESA reported in 2020 a roughly nine-per-cent global-average weakening, yet our atmosphere shields us from radiation like thirteen feet of concrete. Its thin atmosphere has a mean surface pressure of six point three six millibars — under one per cent of Earth's — and an average temperature of minus fifty-nine degrees Celsius. Mars also hosts the Solar System's largest volcano, Olympus Mons, reaching twenty-one point three kilometres above Mars's zero-elevation datum — over twice Mount Everest — across an Arizona-sized base.

After a global dust storm silenced solar-powered Opportunity on 10 June 2018 — exceeding its ninety-Martian-day design life by sixty times — NASA's Ingenuity helicopter completed seventy-two flights in that thin air through 18 January 2024. What looms beyond the asteroid belt?

Beyond the asteroid belt at seven hundred and seventy-eight million kilometres — five point two astronomical units — looms Jupiter. Holding nearly three hundred and eighteen Earth masses, more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined, it spans eleven times wider than Earth — a basketball beside a grape.

However, Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet, spinning in nine point nine hours on a twelve-Earth-year orbit. In 1610, Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei spotted its four largest moons. Meanwhile, in Jupiter's southern sky swirls the Great Red Spot — a storm wider than Earth measured since the late 1800s as it shrank from about forty-one thousand kilometres to under sixteen thousand five hundred in 2014.

Why are Saturn's rings vanishing?

At one point four billion kilometres — nine point five astronomical units — orbits Saturn. Nine times wider than Earth — a volleyball beside a nickel — Saturn spins in ten point seven hours at six hundred and eighty-seven kilograms per cubic metre, the only planet less dense than water.

Its ring system extends up to two hundred and eighty-two thousand kilometres from the planet, yet the main rings stand about ten metres thick. Why are they vanishing? During 2017 dives between the innermost D ring and cloud tops, Cassini measured ring material pouring into Saturn at four thousand eight hundred to forty-five thousand kilograms per second, while six gravity crossings weighed them at zero point four one Mimas masses — indicating they may have formed ten to one hundred million years ago.
